summary.title: Comparative Performance Analysis of Image De-noising Techniques
summary.authors: Vivek Kumar, Pranay Yadav, Atul Samadhiya, Sandeep Jain, and Prayag Tiwari
summary.executive_summary: This paper provides a comprehensive survey of image noise types and denoising algorithms, culminating in a comparative performance analysis. The authors first categorize noise into additive (Gaussian, Salt and Pepper) and multiplicative (Speckle, Brownian) types, detailing their statistical properties and visual characteristics. Subsequently, they classify denoising techniques into spatial filtering (linear and non-linear) and transform domain filtering (spatial-frequency and wavelet-based). The study highlights the trade-offs between noise reduction and edge preservation, noting that linear filters often blur edges while non-linear and wavelet methods offer better structural retention. A quantitative evaluation is performed on a grayscale Lena image corrupted with 90% noise density. Results indicate that while Mean Filters (MF) and Adaptive Mean Filters (AMF) yield poor Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratios (PSNR) of 6.58 and 8.06 respectively, advanced wavelet-based methods like MDBUTMF achieve a superior PSNR of 17.99. The paper concludes that algorithm selection is application-dependent and suggests future research directions in adaptive thresholding and shift-invariant transforms.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper provides a comprehensive survey of image noise types and denoising algorithms, culminating in a comparative performance analysis. The authors first categorize noise into additive (Gaussian, Salt and Pepper) and multiplicative (Speckle, Brownian) types, detailing their statistical properties and visual characteristics. Subsequently, they classify denoising techniques into spatial filtering (linear and non-linear) and transform domain filtering (spatial-frequency and wavelet-based). The study highlights the trade-offs between noise reduction and edge preservation, noting that linear filters often blur edges while non-linear and wavelet methods offer better structural retention. A quantitative evaluation is performed on a grayscale Lena image corrupted with 90% noise density. Results indicate that while Mean Filters (MF) and Adaptive Mean Filters (AMF) yield poor Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratios (PSNR) of 6.58 and 8.06 respectively, advanced wavelet-based methods like MDBUTMF achieve a superior PSNR of 17.99. The paper concludes that algorithm selection is application-dependent and suggests future research directions in adaptive thresholding and shift-invariant transforms.

Research Context
Image restoration addresses degradations like blurring and noise. Noise corrupts images from electronic and photometric sources. Effective denoising requires knowledge of the specific noise type. Existing literature lacks a unified comparative study of algorithms.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study aims to classify noise types and evaluate denoising algorithms. Different noise types require specific algorithmic approaches. Wavelet-based methods are hypothesized to outperform spatial filters. Advanced wavelet thresholds reduce artifacts compared to hard thresholding. Performance will be measured using PSNR and IEF metrics.

Methodological Details
The study analyzes various noise types including Gaussian and Speckle. Gaussian noise is evenly distributed over the signal. Salt and pepper noise is an impulse type with two values. Speckle noise is multiplicative and follows a gamma distribution. Brownian noise is a fractal or 1/f noise type. Denoising is classified into spatial and transform domain methods. Spatial filters are divided into linear and non-linear categories. Transform domain methods use FFT and wavelet transforms. The evaluation uses a grayscale Lena image with 90% noise. Performance is quantified using PSNR and Image Enhancement Factor.

Procedures And Architectures
Linear filters are optimal for Gaussian noise in mean square error. Wiener filtering requires knowledge of noise and signal spectra. Wavelet domain filtering separates signal from noise via coefficients. Hard thresholding removes small coefficients but creates artifacts. Soft thresholding shrinks coefficients above the threshold. VISU Shrink uses a universal threshold dependent on pixel count. SURE Shrink combines universal and Stein's Unbiased Risk Estimator. Bayes Shrink minimizes Bayes Risk assuming generalized Gaussian prior. Un-decimated Wavelet Transform avoids visual artifacts like Gibbs. Multiwavelets enhance performance but increase computation complexity.

Key Results
Mean Filter achieved the lowest PSNR of 6.5759. Adaptive Mean Filter improved PSNR to 8.0603. PSMF filter yielded a PSNR of 6.7847. DBA method achieved a PSNR of 17.1205. MDBA method achieved a PSNR of 17.2242. MDBUTMF achieved the highest PSNR of 17.9865. MDBUTMF also achieved the highest IEF of 16.2066. MDBA achieved an IEF of 13.5976. DBA achieved an IEF of 13.2768. MF had the lowest IEF of 1.1712.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
Simple linear filters fail to preserve edges effectively. Wavelet methods exploit multi-resolution properties for better results. Adaptive thresholds outperform non-adaptive universal thresholds. Shift invariance reduces visual artifacts in wavelet transforms. High noise density (90%) stresses the robustness of algorithms. MDBUTMF demonstrates superior performance in this specific setup.

Contradictions And Limitations
The study relies on a single test image (Lena). Results are specific to 90% noise density. Computational complexity limits the use of advanced wavelets. The paper is a survey rather than an experimental validation.

Claims
Wavelet-based denoising outperforms traditional spatial filtering in high-noise scenarios. MDBUTMF achieved the highest PSNR of 17.9865. Linear filters tend to blur sharp edges. Un-decimated Wavelet Transform adds large computational overhead. Algorithm selection depends on application constraints.
Adaptive thresholding methods reduce artifacts compared to hard thresholding. Soft thresholding shrinks coefficients above the threshold. Hard thresholding generates spurious blips. Bayes Shrink outperforms SURE Shrink most of the times. Statistical modeling improves exact representation of image data.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The study evaluates robustness against 90% noise density.

Key Figures Tables
Table I compares PSNR and IEF for different filters. Fig. 1 illustrates Gaussian distribution. Fig. 4 illustrates Salt and Pepper noise. Fig. 6 illustrates Speckle noise. Fig. 8 illustrates Brownian noise.

Three Takeaways
1. Wavelet-based methods like MDBUTMF significantly outperform linear filters. 2. Algorithm selection must account for noise type and computational cost. 3. Future work should address computational complexity of shift-invariant transforms.
